title: La vacuna española para la dermatitis: "Los hallazgos invitan a estudiarla"
content: The research team from the Complutense University of Madrid, led by Óscar Palomares and José Luis Subiza, reports that the sublingual bacterial vaccine MV130—previously shown to reduce infant bronchiolitis—also prevents and treats eosinophilic allergic asthma in pre‑clinical murine models.  In mice sensitised to house dust mite (HDM), MV130 both blocked allergic sensitisation and, when given after disease onset, lowered clinical symptoms and restored airway homeostasis.  The authors note that MV130 confers protection for up to nine weeks post‑treatment in mice, which could translate into years of prevention in humans, and that phase‑III trials have shown a reduction in bronchiolitis rates for up to six months after therapy.  By contrast, allergen‑specific immunotherapy (ITA) typically offers protection for about two years after three years of treatment, relying on antigen‑specific mechanisms such as IgG4 and IgA antibodies.  MV130, however, induces trained innate immunity and reprograms human dendritic cells in an antigen‑independent manner, activating TNF‑α, IFN‑γ, IL‑6 and IL‑10 pathways, increasing glycolysis and reducing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.  These metabolic and transcriptomic changes are proposed as potential biomarkers for future clinical trials.  The investigators argue that children at high risk of asthma—those with genetic susceptibility and HDM sensitisation—represent the ideal first‑human cohort, while adolescents and adults with established eosinophilic asthma could be studied for symptom reduction and prevention of severe disease.  They also highlight the possibility of a dual benefit: reducing virus‑triggered exacerbations and controlling eosinophilic inflammation, and suggest exploring booster doses or extended regimens to prolong protection.  Finally, the authors propose extending MV130 research to other eosinophil‑mediated chronic inflammatory conditions such as allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis, citing its ability to inhibit eosinophil recruitment without affecting resident pulmonary eosinophils.

title: El estiramiento de la piel permite la administración de vacunas sin...
content: A study by INSERM and King’s College London, published in *Cell Reports*, shows that stretching the skin can enhance the delivery and immune response to vaccines without needles. The researchers used a suction‑based device that, after 20 minutes of application, temporarily increased skin permeability in mice and humans by opening hair follicles and reorganising collagen fibres. The effect lasted about 15 minutes before the skin returned to its normal barrier function. In mice, the stretch induced a local immune response: 24 hours after treatment, there was a marked rise in immune cells in the skin and over 1,000 genes, including cytokine‑encoding genes, were differentially expressed. When a topical flu vaccine (H1N1) was applied with the device, the vaccine entered the bloodstream slowly and accumulated in nearby lymph nodes, leading to higher antibody titres than intramuscular injection. Adding an adjuvant did not further boost the response, suggesting the mechanical stretch alone was sufficient. The lead author, Elodie Segura, cautioned that while the method shows promise, it could also allow toxic compounds or trigger unwanted inflammation: 'Hay que tener mucho cuidado con lo que se aplica en la piel'. Stuart Jones added, 'Tan solo estirar la skin fue más efectivo que administrar la misma vacuna con una aguja', highlighting the practical potential of this needle‑free approach. The authors note that further research is needed to confirm similar effects in humans and to assess safety.

title: Vaccination : bientôt une alternative sans piqûre grâce au massage
content: Researchers from Inserm, the Curie Institute, and King’s College London investigated whether skin massage could serve as a needle‑free vaccination method. The study, conducted on mice, involved a 20‑minute massage using a device that stretched the skin without causing lesions. The massage produced a tension comparable to therapeutic massage with cream, temporarily increasing skin permeability to macromolecules by opening hair follicles. This allowed large vaccine molecules to penetrate the dermis, triggering a local inflammatory response and initiating an immune reaction in the mice. The results suggest that massage could be a viable alternative to injectable vaccines.

title: Fini les piqûres, des chercheurs inventent le vaccin injecté par massage : Actualités - Orange
content: A September 2025 study published in Cell Reports by researchers from Inserm, the Institut Curie, and King's College London introduces a needle-free vaccination method using mechanical stress from massage or a small suction device. The research shows that mechanical pressure, similar to that applied during topical cream application, can dilate the skin sufficiently to allow vaccine molecules to enter through hair follicle cavities. According to Elodie Segura, cited in Le Monde, immune cells detect changes in skin force and trigger an immune response by dilating the skin. This process enables vaccine molecules—along with naturally occurring skin bacteria—to penetrate and initiate immunity. While manual massage proved more effective than the prototype suction device in experiments, researchers developed the tool to standardize the method and eliminate dependence on human variation. The innovation aims to address widespread needle phobia, reported in 20–50% of adolescents and 10% of the general population who avoid vaccination due to fear of injections, according to the National Center for Biotechnology Information and Le Monde.

title: Needle-Free Vaccine Delivery Enabled by Stretching the Skin
content:
Researchers from INSERM and King’s College London demonstrated that mechanically stretching the skin can activate local immune responses and temporarily increase skin permeability without causing tissue damage. Using a suction‑based device that applies pressure for 20 minutes, the team showed that the stretch rearranges collagen fibers, opens hair follicles, and allows large molecules to penetrate. In both mouse and human skin, permeability to fluorescently labeled macromolecules rose for about 15 minutes before returning to baseline. The device also induced a local inflammatory response: 24 hours after stretching, immune cell numbers in the skin were higher, and dendritic cells migrated to draining lymph nodes. Gene‑expression analysis revealed 498 genes up‑regulated and 593 down‑regulated, many encoding cytokines. When a topical flu vaccine was applied concurrently with skin stretching, mice exhibited a slow, controlled uptake of the antigen into the bloodstream and higher antibody titres against H1N1 compared with intramuscular injection; adding an adjuvant did not further enhance the response. The authors concluded that a single stretch can trigger mechanosensing, inflammation, and immune cell recruitment, and that the reversible opening of hair follicles offers a promising route for needle‑free vaccine delivery. They cautioned that the same mechanism could also facilitate penetration of toxins or allergens, warranting further safety studies in humans.

Key metrics: 20‑minute stretch increased permeability for ~15 minutes; 498 genes up‑regulated, 593 down‑regulated; antibody levels against H1N1 were higher with the skin‑stretch method than with intramuscular injection.

title: 2025 Human Papillomavirus (HPV) Vaccine Market Evolution: Data-Driven Insights and Forecast to 2034
content: The human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine market is projected to grow from $5.8 billion in 2024 to $6.57 billion in 2025, reflecting a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 13.2%. By 2029, the market is expected to reach $10.7 billion, with a CAGR of 13.0% from 2025 to 2029. Key drivers of growth include increased awareness of HPV-related diseases, government-led vaccination initiatives, healthcare equity efforts, integration into travel health advisories, advancements in adjuvant technology, expanded focus on immunocompromised individuals and LGBTQ+ health, and collaboration with cancer screening programs. The market is segmented by type (Tetravalent, Nonavalent, Bivalent), disease indication (Cervical Cancer, Anal Cancer, etc.), distribution channel (Hospital and Retail Pharmacies, Government Suppliers), and industry vertical (Public and Private Alliance, Government Entities). A notable innovation is CERVAVAC, the first quadrivalent HPV vaccine developed entirely by Indian researchers, introduced by the Serum Institute of India in January 2023. North America was the largest regional market in 2024. Major players include Merck & Co Inc., GlaxoSmithKline Plc, Johnson & Johnson Co, Sanofi SA, Novartis AG, and Serum Institute of India Pvt Ltd. The National Cancer Institute estimates 13,960 new cervical cancer cases and 4,310 deaths in the U.S. in 2023, with incidence and mortality rates of 7.7 and 2.2 per 100,000 women annually, respectively, underscoring the urgency of vaccination.

title: Sivilceye karşı iki aşı yolda
content: Two separate vaccine projects aimed at treating and preventing acne are underway in the United States and France. Sanofi’s first vaccine, produced with mRNA technology used in COVID‑19 shots, introduces genetic fragments from the acne‑causing bacterium 'Cutibacterium acnes' to stimulate antibody production. In animal studies it proved effective, and it is currently being tested on 400 volunteers in the U.S. with moderate to severe acne. The second vaccine targets the enzyme 'hyaluronidase', which facilitates acne formation; by suppressing this enzyme, the vaccine is expected to halt new breakouts. Mouse studies suggest it can reduce acne severity by about 50 %. Clinical results for the first vaccine are anticipated in 2027, while the second vaccine could take up to five years to reach the market. The article notes that acne develops when sebum blocks hair follicles, and that current treatments face issues of antibiotic resistance and side effects.

title: Pourquoi il est important de se faire vacciner contre le zona
content: Vaccination against shingles (zona) is increasingly important as the disease becomes more frequent and severe with age. In France, about one person in four over 75 experiences persistent pain or disabling complications after a shingles episode. The new recombinant vaccine Shingrix, introduced in spring 2024, is reimbursed at 65 % and has a real‑world efficacy of 79.3 %, compared with 45.9 % for the older live‑attenuated vaccine Zostavax, which is no longer available. The Haute autorité en santé (HASHAS) recommends in March 2024 that all adults 65 + who are immunocompetent, and all immunodepressed adults 18 + (including those with HIV, organ transplants, cancer or chronic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, lupus or inflammatory bowel disease), receive Shingrix. The vaccination schedule is two intramuscular doses spaced at least two months apart, up to six months; if the interval is exceeded, a single additional dose suffices. People who have had shingles or were previously vaccinated with Zostavax should receive a full Shingrix series after at least one year. Shingles manifests as a painful, vesicular rash that usually affects one side of the thorax or abdomen in a 'half-belt' pattern; it can also involve the face (ophthalmic shingles) or cause complications such as post‑herpetic neuralgia, which affects about 25 % of people over 75. The disease occurs in 5–10 cases per 1 000 people aged 60 + per year. About 90 % of cases heal after 2–3 weeks of vesicle outbreaks, but antiviral treatment must be started within three days of rash onset to be effective. Shingles can lead to serious complications such as facial paralysis, dysphagia, urinary retention or hearing loss. The new vaccine is recommended for all adults 65 + and immunodepressed adults 18 +; it is reimbursed at 65 % by the national health insurance since 14 December 2024.

title: Vaccini Anziani 2025 Italia: Quali sono i Raccomandati per Over 60
content: The 2023-2025 National Vaccination Prevention Plan (PNPV) in Italy emphasizes comprehensive protection for individuals over 60 against severe respiratory infections and other age-specific diseases. Key vaccines recommended and offered free of charge include: 1) Influenza vaccine—recommended annually for all individuals aged 60 and above, with high-dose adjuvanted formulations; 2) Pneumococcal vaccine—strongly recommended and free for those over 65, using conjugated PCV vaccines for long-term protection; 3) Herpes Zoster (shingles) vaccine—recommended and free for all individuals aged 65 and older, with over 90% efficacy and requiring two doses; 4) Updated monovalent COVID-19 vaccine—recommended for individuals aged 60 and older, with annual boosters due to ongoing circulation of SARS-CoV-2; 5) Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) vaccine—newly introduced, recommended for adults aged 60 and above. The Ministry of Health and the National Health Service (SSN) advise co-administration of influenza and COVID-19 vaccines starting in October 2025. Individuals who have had pneumonia are still advised to receive the pneumococcal vaccine. The FAQ section confirms that the shingles vaccine requires two doses and that both flu and COVID-19 vaccines can be administered together.

title: Вакцины можно будет вводить дома без использования игл
content: Scientists from the Royal College of London have shown that vaccines can be delivered without needles by stretching the skin. In the experiment, a suction device was applied to mouse and human skin samples for 20 minutes, increasing skin tension from the normal ~1.5 newtons to about 6 newtons. The vaccine absorbed through the stretched skin was taken up as effectively as when injected into the bloodstream. The study compared intramuscular injection of a flu vaccine with skin stretching followed by application of a lotion containing the same dose. In mice, the immune response was comparable, and the local vaccine worked effectively both with and without an adjuvant. The researchers suggest that in the future people could self‑administer vaccines at home using a small device that applies tension to the skin, eliminating the need for blood and skin damage. As the study notes, 'In the future, vaccines could be administered without needles.'
